text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Tax Minister Thomas Ostros has dismissed a proposal to cut taxes on services as it lacks sufficient financing. Dan Andersson, who has been appointed to look into the matter, will present the proposal to the government on Monday.

- A communication ministry expert says it is worrying that the three-nation committee investigating the sinking of the ferry Estonia in the Baltic Sea in September 1994 cannot agree. The Estonian chairman of the committee, Uno Laur, has freed the Estonian crew from acting wrongly at the time of the accident while the Swedish and Finnish chairmen do not seem to accept this. A total of 852 people died in the catastrophe.

- A committee looking into how society can combat child pornography will present a proposal on Monday that largely leaves children without any legal rights and gives paedophiles protection, a law professor said in a column.
- Eight unions and five employer organisations will sign a cooperation agreement on Monday in an attempt to avoid labour market conflicts.
- People critical towards a proposal about how to combat child pornography will stage a large demonstration on April 26, calling for a total ban on such material.

- Merger talks between S-E-Banken and Nordbanken are not likely to be resumed until after S-E-Banken's annual general shareholders' meeting on April 29, sources told the newspaper. S-E-Banken's share closed at a record 84.50 crowns on Friday on the Stockholm Stock Exchange on rumours of a merger with Nordbanken. The banks ended merger talks without reaching any conclusions earlier this year, but analysts expect talks to start again. The newspaper reported on Saturday that chairman of Swedish bank Swedbank expected Nordbanken and S-E-Banken to merge.

- This week companies will start paying out dividends with 30 of the largest companies on the bourse to give 31.1 billion crowns to shareholders this spring. Of this amount, 22.1 billion crowns will be paid out to Swedish owners and 9.0 billion to overseas interests. The dividend payouts are almost 22 percent higher than a year ago.
